item.text: {"text":"[Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008v1) evaluates 15 datasets using sequential-rule counts, HR@10/NDCG@10 degradation, and recommendation-list Jaccard@10. Its model probes train SASRec and GRU4Rec on chronological data, then shuffle evaluation histories while retaining held-out targets. Several datasets show little degradation; others show substantial losses. Crucially, retaining the target does not retain the most recent input item: full-history shuffling changes both earlier order and the item occupying the final position. Thus, the experiment does not isolate broader order dependence from last-item or recency effects.\n\nRecommended controls—methodological inference, rather than controls established by that paper: compare original histories, fully shuffled histories, prefix shuffling with the final input item fixed, and prefix shuffling with the last several inputs fixed. Preserve history membership, padding, targets, candidates, and readout position; repeat permutations to quantify uncertainty. For GRU4Rec, use the final nonpadding position under left padding. A full-shuffle loss that disappears when the last item is fixed supports sensitivity to the latest item; residual loss supports sensitivity to earlier positional arrangement, but still cannot distinguish recency weighting from higher-order transitions. Evaluation-only shuffling also introduces distribution shift, so degradation establishes perturbation sensitivity—not proof of learned higher-order sequential structure. Matched chronological-versus-shuffled training/evaluation controls can help separate these explanations; [Woolridge et al. (2021)](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2955/paper8.pdf) provide a related retraining-based approach."}
